extracted.intended_audience: faculty, administrators, graduate students, and higher-education stakeholders (especially in the humanities and social sciences)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and implementing values-based metrics and evaluation processes for faculty hiring, promotion, tenure, and rewards in humanities and social sciences departments and institutions. Emphasizes participatory workshops to identify institutional values and align reward mechanisms with those values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify core institutional values
rubrics_metrics.description: Help organizations identify their core values and align reward mechanisms with those values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshops ask participants to surface values (e.g., depth, breadth, equity, well-being, intentionality, self-care, empathy, reciprocity, transparency, humility, inclusivity, public good, reproducibility, risk-taking, learning from failure, originality, imagination, accountability), organize them into categories, and rank categories by importance. The process is collaborative and local: “There is no universal framework. The goal ... is simply to engage scholars and administrators in the process of tearing apart, interrogating, and rebuilding a values framework.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess how policies and practices express values
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether institutional policies and everyday practices reflect the institution's stated values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshop prompts move from abstract principles to concrete practices by asking 'What are our most closely held values at the UI? How do our policies and practices express those values?' Use small-group reflection to examine how values currently play out in professional lives and institutional processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the degree to which values are put into practice as an indicator of quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality should be judged by 'the degree to which we put our values into practice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Christopher Long's formulation: 'That is the indicator of quality—the degree to which we put our values into practice.' Use enacted values (not just stated ones) as a central evaluative criterion when assessing work and career trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value the scholarly process as well as the final product
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation should recognize the process of conducting scholarship (where much learning occurs) as well as final outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include and reward activities such as peer review, syllabus development, conference organizing, mentorship, and other time-consuming scholarly practices. Workshop participants suggested rewarding publication of failures and counting citations appearing in syllabi (which reach broader audiences) as alternative indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize collaborative, inclusive, and public-good labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics must capture labor devoted to collaboration, inclusivity, and contributing to the public good—work often neglected by quantitative measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include digital projects built collaboratively, community-engaged projects producing material benefits (e.g., food pantries plus white papers), exhibitions mining community archives, and other efforts that lack conventional publication profiles but advance institutional values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate quality (not merely quantity) of service and mentoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the quality of contributions to committee work, mentoring, and service rather than counting participation or number of committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece contrasts 'quality of a faculty member’s contributions to committee work and mentoring' with the 'number of committees one serves on.' Committees and reviewers should judge effectiveness, impact, and the substance of contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward leadership and stewardship over personal productivity metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for leadership behaviors and sacrifices made for the department or university (e.g., chairs who prioritize others’ success) when evaluating performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize activities like nominating colleagues for awards, writing grants to enrich programs, and other stewardship that may reduce an individual's traditional research output but benefit the institution broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage risk-taking, innovation, and interdisciplinary work
rubrics_metrics.description: Design evaluation systems that do not penalize risk-taking, interdisciplinary, collaborative, digital, or public-engaged scholarship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overvaluing single-authored, discipline-bound outputs; allow credit for newer forms (digital projects, interdisciplinary journals) that may lack immediate prestige. The current emphasis on single-authored publications can discourage untenured scholars from innovative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include invisible and time-consuming labor in assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Make visible and credit the often-invisible labor that sustains academic life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly count and evaluate labor such as peer review, syllabus creation, mentoring, conference organizing, and other intellectual leadership tasks that are time-consuming but critical to institutional health—especially as this labor is disproportionately shouldered by women and people of color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on blunt quantitative metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject narrow counting metrics (e.g., grant dollars, journal status, citation counts, Twitter mentions) as sole determinants of excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace how industrial-era counting shaped modern metrics; recognize that blunt metrics miss important dimensions and can produce perverse incentives. Strive for a balance between quantity and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop qualitative and alternative indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Use both qualitative and alternative quantitative indicators to capture diverse forms of contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshop examples: count citations in syllabi, reward publication of failures, craft indicators that value process and reach. Committees should brainstorm metrics appropriate to the forms of contribution in their units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use participatory, campus-wide processes to define values and indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Include faculty, staff, graduate students, libraries, and other campus actors in defining values and assessment metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The HuMetrics approach emphasizes inclusive workshops and institutional adoption so that individuals can 'talk about the intentionality and values behind their work' and so that institutional frameworks exist before individual evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed values in hiring, goal-setting, and review conversations
rubrics_metrics.description: Start values conversations during hiring and use agreed-upon values to set performance goals and frame review questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change review questions from 'How many publications do you have?' to 'How have you shared knowledge, expanded opportunity, and stewarded resources? What does the arc of your career look like over the next five years?' Use values as a lodestar for supervisors and review committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify governance: who determines promotion and tenure policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve confusion about who sets and enforces promotion and tenure policies and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the HuMetrics 'to do' list is to 'clear up confusion about who determines promotion and tenure policies and outcomes' so stakeholders know where authority and responsibility lie and can act to change processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide tools and infrastructure for implementing values-based assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Create practical toolkits and digital tools to help institutions run workshops and measure overlooked indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HuMetrics will make documents and processes open-access, produce a toolkit for running HuMetrics-style workshops, and develop digital tools to help review committees measure indicators like syllabus citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismantle the culture of fear tied to prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Address and reduce the fear of losing prestige or national standing that drives return to narrow statistical measures.
